summary.text: Case 1 is a woman aged 30 of Kurdish ethnicity, admitted to the neurology ward of Tohid Hospital of Sanandaj in July-August 2014-2015 as one of nine patients with cerebral venous thrombosis. The series states that all patients had used a short course oral contraceptive pill during Ramadan to delay women’s menstruation. Table 1 lists headache, vertigo, nausea, vomiting, papilledema, blurred vision and seizure as clinical manifestations.

Table 1 records cerebral venous thrombosis with the involved veins or sinus listed as superior sagittal sinus, bilateral cortical. Predisposing factors were listed as absent, and the table footnote states that predisposing factors, including coagulative disorders and inflammatory diseases, were evaluated and excluded.

Treatment listed in Table 1 was heparin and then warfarin and anticonvulsant. The hospital discharge outcome was recovered, the duration of hospital stay was 6 (no unit printed) and the follow-up period was 6 months.

summary.text: Case 2 is a woman aged 37 of Kurdish ethnicity, admitted to the neurology ward of Tohid Hospital of Sanandaj in July-August 2014-2015 as one of nine patients with cerebral venous thrombosis. The series states that all patients had used a short course oral contraceptive pill during Ramadan to delay women’s menstruation. Table 1 lists headache, vertigo, nausea, vomiting and bilateral papilledema as clinical manifestations.

Table 1 records cerebral venous thrombosis with the involved veins or sinus listed as superior sagittal sinus. Predisposing factors were listed as absent, and the table footnote states that predisposing factors, including coagulative disorders and inflammatory diseases, were evaluated and excluded.

Treatment listed in Table 1 was enoxaparin and then warfarin. The hospital discharge outcome was recovered, the duration of hospital stay was 8 (no unit printed) and the follow-up period was 6 months.

summary.text: Case 5 is a woman aged 25 of Kurdish ethnicity, admitted to the neurology ward of Tohid Hospital of Sanandaj in July-August 2014-2015 as one of nine patients with cerebral venous thrombosis. The series states that all patients had used a short course oral contraceptive pill during Ramadan to delay women’s menstruation. Table 1 lists headache, vertigo, tinnitus, numbness of left face and limbs especially foot, muscle weakness and seizure as clinical manifestations.

Table 1 records cerebral venous thrombosis with the involved veins or sinus listed as thrombosis of right transverse (lateral sinus) extending to the jugular vein. Predisposing factors were listed as absent, and the table footnote states that predisposing factors, including coagulative disorders and inflammatory diseases, were evaluated and excluded.

Treatment listed in Table 1 was enoxaparin and then warfarin and anticonvulsant. The hospital discharge outcome was recovered, the duration of hospital stay was 7 (no unit printed) and the follow-up period was 6 months.

summary.text: Case 6 is a woman aged 26 of Kurdish ethnicity, admitted to the neurology ward of Tohid Hospital of Sanandaj in July-August 2014-2015 as one of nine patients with cerebral venous thrombosis. The series states that all patients had used a short course oral contraceptive pill during Ramadan to delay women’s menstruation. Table 1 lists headache, vertigo, blurred vision, diplopia and papilledema as clinical manifestations.

Table 1 records cerebral venous thrombosis with the involved veins or sinus listed as left lateral sinus, bilateral sigmoid sinus and jugular vein. Predisposing factors were listed as absent, and the table footnote states that predisposing factors, including coagulative disorders and inflammatory diseases, were evaluated and excluded.
Treatment listed in Table 1 was heparin and then warfarin. The hospital discharge outcome was recovered, the duration of hospital stay was 9 (no unit printed) and the follow-up period was 6 months.

summary.text: Case 7 is a woman aged 34 of Kurdish ethnicity, admitted to the neurology ward of Tohid Hospital of Sanandaj in July-August 2014-2015 as one of nine patients with cerebral venous thrombosis. The series states that all patients had used a short course oral contraceptive pill during Ramadan to delay women’s menstruation. Table 1 lists headache, vertigo and vomiting as clinical manifestations.

Table 1 records cerebral venous thrombosis with the involved veins or sinus listed as left lateral sinus. Predisposing factors were listed as absent, and the table footnote states that predisposing factors, including coagulative disorders and inflammatory diseases, were evaluated and excluded.

Treatment listed in Table 1 was enoxaparin and then warfarin. The hospital discharge outcome was recovered, the duration of hospital stay was 6 (no unit printed) and the follow-up period was 8 months.

summary.text: Case 8 is a woman aged 31 of Kurdish ethnicity, admitted to the neurology ward of Tohid Hospital of Sanandaj in July-August 2014-2015 as one of nine patients with cerebral venous thrombosis. The series states that all patients had used a short course oral contraceptive pill during Ramadan to delay women’s menstruation. Table 1 lists headache, low blood pressure, vertigo, nausea, vomiting, papilledema, blurred vision and seizure as clinical manifestations.

Table 1 records cerebral venous thrombosis with the involved veins or sinus listed as left lateral sinus and bilateral sigmoid sinus. Predisposing factors were listed as absent, and the table footnote states that predisposing factors, including coagulative disorders and inflammatory diseases, were evaluated and excluded.

Treatment listed in Table 1 was heparin and then warfarin anticonvulsant. The hospital discharge outcome was recovered, the duration of hospital stay was 15 (no unit printed) and the follow-up period was 18 months.

summary.text: Case 9 is a woman aged 49 of Kurdish ethnicity, admitted to the neurology ward of Tohid Hospital of Sanandaj in July-August 2014-2015 as one of nine patients with cerebral venous thrombosis. The series states that all patients had used a short course oral contraceptive pill during Ramadan to delay women’s menstruation. Table 1 lists low level of consciousness, Glasgow Coma Scale score 3, tachypnea and double Babinski extensor as clinical manifestations.

Table 1 records cerebral venous thrombosis with the involved veins or sinus listed as superior sagittal sinus, left transverse sinus and deep cerebral veins. Obesity with BMI = 35 was listed as the predisposing factor in the Pre-disposing factor column.

Treatment listed in Table 1 was mannitol and dexamethasone. The hospital discharge outcome was expired, due to hemorrhagic infarction, which the table footnote describes as massive hemorrhagic infarctions and thrombosis. The duration of hospital stay was 2 (no unit printed).

article_limitations: Table 1 prints Age and Duration of hospital stay as bare numbers without units, so no years or days are recorded; only the follow-up period column states month.

The Abstract, Methods and Conclusion make unquantified series-level statements (no history of thrombosis, oral contraceptive for more than 1 month to be able to fast, no other possible risk factors, CVT confirmed by magnetic resonance venography, thrombophilia and vasculitis assessments that were rollout, fasting women during Ramadan) without naming individual cases; they are copied to each case only as review_only facts. Statements that explicitly cover all patients (all patients used a short course OCP during Ramadan, nine cases used contraceptive pills to delay menstruation, nine patients with CVT admitted to the neurology ward, headache in 9/9 patients, review_only for Case 9 because the table rows disagree) are recorded for the cases they cover.

Cohort symptom counts and percentages in the Abstract, Discussion and Table 1 footnote (headache 9/9, vomiting 5/9, vertigo 4/9, nausea and seizure 33%, papilledema 33%, blurred vision 22%) agree with the symptoms listed in the Table 1 rows only for some symptoms (nausea and seizure) and disagree for others (for example vertigo, vomiting, papilledema, blurred vision and the headache count). Individual facts follow each patient own row and no count was recalculated or reconciled.

The Introduction says patients were admitted during July-August 2014, while the Abstract and Methods say July-August 2014-2015 (two consecutive years); each admission is recorded only as the stated July-August 2014-2015 window.
Table 1 prints some cells without separators (vomiting papilledema, low blood pressure vertigo, warfarin anticonvulsant); they are read as separate listed items without adding wording.
Figure 1 (brain magnetic resonance venography) is cited only for the series, shows no printed patient label, and is not attributed to any patient; its attribution is unresolved.

The Methods list of the most common clinical signs (headache, papilledema, seizures, sensorimotor deficit, decreased level of consciousness, hemorrhage) is an aggregate statement and is not mapped to individual cases beyond the Table 1 rows; one patient passed away is mapped to Case 9 only through the table cell and footnote that record the single death.

The Case 9 headache comes only from the statements that headache occurred in 9/9 patients; the Case 9 table row does not list it and only eight rows do, so it is kept review_only (count mismatch recorded as an ambiguity).

The Discussion hypothesis about dehydration, comparisons with other published series, regional mortality and incidence figures, and the Introduction general short course pill formulation are not patient facts, and no ingredients or doses are recorded for the cases.
